name: Adam Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for sitting down with me, Adam. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or political parties. What you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. What's a normal working day like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work out of the Millbrook depot, which is a country one, so it's long drives on farm lanes. We look after the rural lines, the wooden poles running out to farms and villages, and most of the work is replacing old poles, fixing what the trees knock down, and changing fuses on the transformers up on poles. I can do forty miles before lunch some days.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's the same job it was when I started, mostly. You know the lanes, you know which farmer will bring you a tea and which one's dog bites. What wears me out is the new systems. Every couple of years they change the job app on the phone, and I just about learn one before it's gone. I don't touch the AI stuff at all, I just ring the control room like I always have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, there you go, all that fuss. Probably at the depot over a brew. I'm not one for posting things online, I've got the phone for calls and the weather.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be glad. Fewer changes to learn, same job, same lanes. We're fine for money, we've got savings and the little flat my aunt left me that we rent out, so it'd just be life carrying on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing, really. Keep turning up, keep the savings where they are, keep the flat let. Maybe I'd finally replace the van at home, I've been putting it off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. That's the one I'd pick if I got to pick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why have you been putting off replacing the van?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Partly money, partly I just don't like change, Carla says. It's a 2011 diesel, it starts every morning. If everything stays calm, I'd get a newer one second-hand, same make. Not electric, not yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would be happiest with this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gordon, probably, he's got three years to go. He just wants it quiet. But honestly most of us would. Nobody joined this job because they wanted surprises.

S0.say: I'd say there you go, all that fuss for nothing, most likely over a cup of tea at the depot, since I don't post things online.
S0.think: I'd be glad, because it means fewer new systems to learn and the same job on the same lanes. With savings and the rented flat my aunt left me, life just carries on.
S0.do: Keeps turning up for work, leaves savings where they are and keeps the inherited flat rented out. Finally replaces his old diesel van at home with a newer second-hand one of the same make.
S0.feel: Calm, the outcome he'd pick if he could.
S0.quote: It's a 2011 diesel, it starts every morning.
S0.fieldNote: Adam's comfort comes from routine and from a quiet financial base, including a rented flat. He doesn't use AI at all and still rings the control room. Even small choices, like the van, show how much he prefers the familiar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it makes sense for the office side, and I'd hope they leave the field alone. If drones check the lines, fine, that saves us driving out to look. I wouldn't make a big speech about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it'd bother me. Not because I'd lose my job, there's always a pole down somewhere, but because I'd have to keep learning new kit when I'd rather just do the work. And there's plenty of contractors round here hiring if the company got funny, so I'm not too worried about money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait. I'd let the younger lads try the new tools first and pick it up when I'm told I have to. I'd keep the savings as they are. If it got really bad at Millbrook, I'd look at one of the contractors, but I'd not go looking yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I suppose. A sort of mild nagging, like a squeak in the van you can't find.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd pick it up when you're told you have to. What happens if you fall behind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd ask Jas, she's young and she's good with it, and she'd show me. I'd buy her lunch. That's how it works, I'm good on the old kit and she's good on the new. Between us we're one decent lineworker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your kids about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leo's thirteen and he'd tell me, not the other way round. I'd tell them to get a trade, same as me. People will always need someone to come out when the lights go off.

S1.say: I'd say it makes sense on the office side and I'd hope they leave fieldwork alone, though drones checking lines would save some driving.
S1.think: It would bother me because I'd have to keep learning new kit, not because I'd lose my job. Plenty of contractors nearby are hiring, so money isn't the worry.
S1.do: Waits and lets younger colleagues try new tools first, learning them only when required. Keeps savings as they are and would consider a contractor job only if things got bad at his depot.
S1.feel: Mildly uneasy, like a squeak in the van he can't track down.
S1.quote: I'm good on the old kit and she's good on the new. Between us we're one decent lineworker.
S1.fieldNote: His unease is about effort and change, not money or job loss. He leans on a younger colleague for new tech and is open about it. He sees the many local contractors as a safety net.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I don't believe it until I see it. A robot up a rotten pole in a muddy field in January, with a bull watching? Show me. That's what I'd say at the depot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: But privately, if it's true, it's bad. Two years is nothing. I'd be forty-five, with two kids at school and the mortgage, and I've never done anything else. The flat rent would help but it doesn't cover the mortgage, and if nobody's working, who's renting?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop spending on anything we don't need, straight away. No new van, no holiday. I'd keep every penny in savings and pay a bit extra on the mortgage. I wouldn't know what to retrain into, so I'd keep working as long as they'd have me and see where it goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Properly. I'd be short with the kids, I know I would.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be short with the kids. Can you picture a moment?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nina asks a lot of questions at tea. I'd be tired, I'd have heard something at work, and I'd snap at her for nothing. Then I'd feel terrible and go and sit in the van for ten minutes. I've done it before, when Dad was ill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd keep working and see where it goes. Is that a plan, or is that waiting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's waiting. I know. But I don't know what a plan looks like if everything's changed. I'm not going to throw money at some course that's out of date before I finish it.

S2.say: I'd say I won't believe it until I see a robot up a rotten pole in a muddy field in January, and that's what I'd tell people at the depot.
S2.think: If it's true it's bad, because two years is nothing and I've never done anything else. The flat's rent wouldn't cover the mortgage, and fewer people working means fewer renters.
S2.do: Cuts all non-essential spending at once, dropping the van and the holiday. Keeps savings intact, pays extra on the mortgage and keeps working while waiting to see what happens.
S2.feel: Properly anxious, enough to be short-tempered with his children.
S2.quote: It's waiting. I know. But I don't know what a plan looks like if everything's changed.
S2.fieldNote: His public line is disbelief, but privately he takes the threat seriously. When asked whether waiting is a plan, he admitted it isn't. His savings and the flat cushion him, which keeps him short of alarm, but he can't picture retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let's see how it goes, five years is a long time. Things get announced and then they take twice as long. That's my line on most things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be thinking about the numbers. Five years more pay, the mortgage down a fair bit, savings up. I'd be forty-eight. That's a better place to be hit from than forty-five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pay extra on the mortgage every month, a couple of hundred, from the first month. Keep the flat let. Watch what the company does, and if they start testing robots at Millbrook, I'd ask what jobs there are looking after them. I'd only go on a course if the company paid and it was for a job they'd actually give me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Still a worry, but not the knot in my stomach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need to see before you'd take a course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A real job at the end. Someone from the company saying, Adam, do this course and you'll run the robot truck at Millbrook. Not a leaflet. I've seen leaflets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Carla about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're alright, love, we just keep chipping at the mortgage. She'd be the one with a spreadsheet. She's better at that than me.

S3.say: I'd say let's see how it goes, since five years is a long time and announced changes usually take twice as long.
S3.think: I'd be thinking about numbers: five more years of pay, a smaller mortgage and bigger savings. Being hit at forty-eight is better than at forty-five.
S3.do: Pays a couple of hundred extra on the mortgage every month from the start and keeps the flat rented. Asks about robot-maintenance roles if the depot begins testing robots, but only takes a course the company pays for with a real job at the end.
S3.feel: Uneasy, still worried but without the knot in his stomach.
S3.quote: Someone from the company saying, Adam, do this course and you'll run the robot truck at Millbrook. Not a leaflet. I've seen leaflets.
S3.fieldNote: Extra time softens him a lot because he thinks in years of pay and mortgage. He'd retrain only with a guaranteed job, which reflects his risk-averse nature. His partner handles the household planning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years, that's practically retirement for half the depot. I'd say it as a joke, but I'd mean it a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years I can live with. I'd be fifty-three, mortgage nearly gone, kids grown, the flat paid for. If they let me go then, I'd get by on the rent and whatever pay-off they give. I'd call that an early retirement, not a disaster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working. Keep paying down the mortgage. Maybe in a few years I'd look at buying a second little flat with the savings, if prices made sense, so there's a bit more coming in. I wouldn't change jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, the background kind. Like a long weather forecast that might be wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A second flat. Who would rent it if lots of people lost work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good question. I don't know. That's why I said if prices made sense. If it all looked wobbly I'd leave the money in the bank. Carla would decide, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jas. She's twenty-six. She'd be thirty-six when it lands, with maybe kids of her own. She's the one who's good with the tech, but it's people her age who'd have to start again. I'd be alright. She wouldn't, maybe.

S4.say: I’d joke at the depot that ten years is practically retirement for half the crew there. It would be a joke, but I’d half mean it.
S4.think: Ten years I can live with, because at fifty-three the mortgage would be nearly gone and the flat paid for. If they let me go then, I'd call it early retirement rather than a disaster.
S4.do: Keeps working and paying down the mortgage without changing jobs. Considers using savings to buy a second small rental flat in a few years, but only if prices make sense.
S4.feel: A background unease, like a long-range forecast that might be wrong.
S4.quote: She's the one who's good with the tech, but it's people her age who'd have to start again.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years he can see a path to an early retirement funded by rent. His worry shifts to a younger colleague who'd face the change mid-career. He's unsure about buying more property when challenged and hands the decision to his partner.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. What would help is the company being straight with us, telling us early what's changing and which jobs stay. And if there's a course, let it come with a job. I don't need much more than that.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe the farmers. Half of them only see a person from the outside world when we come out to fix the line. A robot won't stop for a tea and ask how the lambing went.

headlineQuote: A robot won't stop for a tea and ask how the lambing went.
portrait: Adam Santos is a 43-year-old lineworker at a rural depot, driving farm lanes to replace poles and fix storm damage, married to Carla, who works at the council, with two children. He has solid savings and a small rented flat inherited from his aunt, and he never uses AI, preferring to ring the control room. He's calm if nothing changes and only mildly uneasy with steady change, leaning on a younger colleague for new tech. Fast AGI makes him anxious and he admits his response is just waiting, but with five or ten years he relaxes into paying off the mortgage and sees a possible early retirement.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because two years leaves no time to get ahead of the mortgage or find something else.
whatWouldHelp: The company being straight and early about which jobs stay, and any retraining course coming with a real job at the end.
